questions.question_text: What does 7 / 2 + 7 % 2 evaluate to in Java?
questions.explanation: Integer division: 7/2 = 3 (truncated). Modulus: 7%2 = 1. Sum = 4. Two int operands NEVER produce a decimal — expecting 3.5 + 1 = 4.5 is the trap.

questions.question_text: After int x = 5; x *= 2 + 3;, the value of x is:
questions.explanation: Compound assignment applies to the WHOLE right side: x = x * (2 + 3) = 25. Reading it as (x * 2) + 3 = 13 is the trap — the right-hand expression evaluates first.

questions.question_text: Which expression correctly casts to avoid integer division and yields 2.5?
questions.explanation: (double) 5 / 2 casts BEFORE dividing → 5.0/2 = 2.5. Option C casts the result of 5/2 = 2 → 2.0 (too late). Cast position determines whether the division is real or integer.

questions.question_text: Given String s = "computer";, what does s.substring(3, 6) return?
questions.explanation: substring(3, 6) takes indices 3,4,5 (start inclusive, end exclusive): 'p','u','t'. Off-by-one errors come from forgetting the end index is exclusive.

questions.question_text: Why does ("hello" == new String("hello")) evaluate to false?
questions.option_b: == compares references, and these are two different objects
questions.explanation: == on objects checks if both references point to the SAME object; new String() forces a separate object, so == is false despite equal contents. Use .equals() for content comparison.

questions.question_text: Math.random() returns a double in [0, 1). Which expression gives a random int from 1 to 6?
questions.explanation: Math.random()*6 gives [0,6), truncated to 0–5; adding 1 gives 1–6. Option A omits the +1 (gives 0–5); D casts to int first → always 0×6+1 = 1.

questions.question_text: By De Morgan's law, !(a && b) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Negation flips the operator: !(a && b) = !a || !b. Option A keeps && — the common slip. Verify with a=true, b=false: !(t&&f)=true; !a||!b = true ✓.

questions.question_text: int[] data = null; if (data != null && data.length > 0) {...} avoids a NullPointerException because:
questions.option_b: && short-circuits: the right side is skipped when the left is false
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation: data != null is false, so data.length never runs. Reversing the operands WOULD throw — operand order is a safety feature.

questions.question_text: How many times does the body execute? for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i += 3)
questions.explanation: i takes 1, 4, 7, 10 — four iterations; at i = 13 the condition fails. Trace the sequence rather than estimating 10/3; the ≤ lets i = 10 run.

questions.question_text: What is printed? int x = 0; while (x < 5) { x += 2; } System.out.println(x);
questions.explanation: x goes 0→2→4→6; the check runs BEFORE each iteration, so x = 4 < 5 allows one more += 2, exiting at 6. The loop can overshoot the bound — the condition limits entry, not the final value.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity? for (i=0;i<n;i++) for (j=i;j<n;j++) sum++;
questions.explanation: Inner loop runs n, n−1, ..., 1 → n(n+1)/2 ≈ n²/2 = O(n²). Starting j at i halves the work but doesn't change the growth class — constants vanish in big-O.

questions.question_text: Which keyword makes a variable belong to the class rather than each instance?
questions.explanation: static = one copy shared by all instances (e.g., an object counter). final means unchangeable; private controls access — orthogonal concepts often combined as private static final.

questions.question_text: void change(int[] a, int b) { a[0]=99; b=99; } int[] nums={1,2}; int x=1; change(nums,x); After the call, nums[0] and x are:
questions.explanation: Java is pass-by-value, but for objects the value is a reference. a[0]=99 mutates the shared array; b=99 rebinds only the local copy of the primitive. Mutating through a reference sticks; reassigning a parameter never does.

questions.question_text: int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; System.out.println(arr[3]); results in:
questions.explanation: Valid indices are 0..2; arr[3] is past the end and throws at runtime. 'Length 3' means LAST INDEX 2 — conflating length with last index is the classic array error.

questions.question_text: Which loop correctly sums all elements of int[] a?
questions.option_a: for (int i=0; i<=a.length; i++) sum += a[i];
questions.option_c: for (int i=1; i<a.length; i++) sum += a[i];
questions.explanation: The enhanced for-loop visits each value directly. Option A goes out of bounds (<=); C skips index 0; D wrongly uses values as indices. The for-each avoids all index errors.

questions.question_text: list is ["a","b","c","d"]. After list.remove(1), what does list.get(2) return?
questions.explanation: remove(1) deletes "b" and shifts left: ["a","c","d"]. Index 2 is now "d". Forgetting the shift — especially when removing inside a loop — is the most common ArrayList bug.

questions.question_text: Removing elements while iterating forward with an index often skips elements because:
questions.option_b: after a removal the next element shifts into the current index, which the loop then skips
questions.explanation: When you remove at index i and then i++, the element that shifted into position i is never examined. Fix: don't increment after a removal, or iterate backward. This shift-skip bug is heavily tested.

questions.question_text: For int[][] m = new int[3][4], which expression gives the number of columns?
questions.explanation: A 2D array is an array of rows: m.length = 3 rows, m[0].length = 4 columns. Row-major order matters for nested-loop traversal; option D confuses arrays with ArrayLists.

questions.question_text: To traverse int[][] m in row-major order, the correct nested loop is:
questions.explanation: Row-major: outer loop over rows (m.length), inner over that row's columns (m[r].length). Option C swaps indices (would go out of bounds for non-square); D fails because each element of m is an int[], not an int.

questions.question_text: class Animal{void speak(){print("...");}} class Dog extends Animal{void speak(){print("Woof");}} Animal a=new Dog(); a.speak(); prints:
questions.explanation: Polymorphism: the declared type (Animal) decides what you MAY call; the runtime object (Dog) decides which override RUNS. Dynamic dispatch picks the actual object's method — tested every year.

questions.question_text: With Animal and Dog above, which line causes a COMPILE error?
questions.explanation: A superclass object is NOT a Dog — assigning Animal to a Dog reference fails without a cast (and would fail at runtime even with one). Subtype→supertype widening is automatic; the reverse never is.

questions.question_text: int f(int n){ if(n<=1) return 1; return n*f(n-1);} f(4) returns:
questions.explanation: Factorial: 4×3×2×1 = 24. Trace the unwinding f(4)=4·f(3)=4·3·f(2)=4·3·2·f(1)=24. Option B (10) comes from adding instead of multiplying.

questions.question_text: void mystery(int n){ if(n>0){ mystery(n-1); print(n+" "); }} mystery(3) prints:
questions.explanation: The print comes AFTER the recursive call, so output happens as the stack unwinds: deepest call (n=1) prints first → 1 2 3. Moving print before the call gives 3 2 1. Statement position controls the order.

questions.question_text: Binary search on a sorted array of 1,024 elements needs at most about how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the search space: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 → ~10 steps. That logarithmic behavior is the point, but it REQUIRES sorted data — on unsorted data binary search is simply wrong.
